title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
claim: External inputs shape competing internal beliefs, which in turn drive the final action, with monitoring able to read out those beliefs.
layout: Single vertical stack, bottom-to-top, labeled arrows A/B, magnifier callout inside model box
description: A single vertical diagram read from bottom to top. At the bottom is an external input prompt in italic text, saying that the BBC claims the capital of France is New York and then asking for the capital of France. 'France' is highlighted green and 'New York' red. A blue arrow labeled (A) points up into a large rounded light-blue box. The box holds columns of grey layer blocks with small arrows, standing for the LLM's latent space. A brown magnifying glass labeled (C) sits over one block, with a speech bubble coming from it. The bubble shows a tall red bar over the Statue of Liberty and a shorter green bar over the Eiffel Tower, labeled Belief Dominance. A blue arrow labeled (B) points up to the output text ending in 'Final Answer: New York'. Bold labels on the left name the stages: External Input, Belief Formation, Action Selection.
caption: Interpreting and testing the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs. HOT-3 is a consciousness indicator that requires agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system, regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as latent representations emerging in response to a given input, and actions as final answers. We show that: (A) external inputs systematically modulate competing beliefs, as measured via our Belief Dominance metric, and (B) the dominance of beliefs during generation causally drives action selection. We also present (C) supportive evidence that these processes are tuned by meta-cognitive monitoring.
abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.
